For anyone holding a lease-end payoff letter

Buy out the lease, or return it and replace it?

The payoff price alone does not answer the question. This compares the true cost per month of use on both paths — buying out against returning and replacing — using the equipment's remaining useful life and what a replacement actually costs.

New to this decision? Read the guide: should I buy out my equipment lease?

This calculator vs. Crest Capital's lease calculator

This calculator vs. comparing the buyout price to fair market value

Your lease and replacement numbers

A comparable listing or appraisal, not the payoff letter's number.

If you return it instead

Cost per month of use

$333.33buying out
$385.00return and replace
$9,240.00break-even buyout price
33%buyout vs. fair market value

    Common questions

    Why isn’t the buyout price alone enough to decide?

    Because a price only means something next to what it buys. A $9,000 buyout is expensive on equipment worth $6,000 with a year of life left, and cheap on equipment that would cost $30,000 to replace and run for five more years. This tool divides the buyout price by the months of use you expect to get, and does the same for a replacement, so the two numbers are comparable on a common footing: cost per month of use.

    Where do I get the fair market value and useful-life numbers?

    They are your own estimate, not a lookup this tool performs. For fair market value, a comparable listing (equipment dealer, auction result, or classifieds for the same make, model, and age) is usually close enough; a written appraisal is better if the number is large. For remaining useful life, your own maintenance history and how hard the equipment has been run matter more than its age on paper. Both numbers drive the verdict directly, so a rough guess in either one should be treated as a rough verdict.

    What is the break-even buyout price?

    The buyout price at which paying it and returning-and-replacing cost exactly the same per month of use. It is the number worth negotiating against, not the figure on the payoff letter — a payoff letter is what the lessor wants, not what the equipment is worth to you. If the quoted buyout is above break-even, walking away is the cheaper path by this estimate; if it is below, paying it is.

    Why does the buyout price sometimes exceed fair market value?

    Some leases set the buyout at a fixed schedule agreed at signing rather than at true fair market value, and a fixed schedule can drift well above what the equipment is actually worth by the time the option is exercised — especially on equipment that depreciates fast. If your lease says the buyout is supposed to be fair market value and the lessor’s number is well above a comparable listing, that is worth raising before paying it, not after.

    What does the replacement side of the comparison include?

    The all-in cost of a comparable replacement — purchase price or the total of a new lease — plus removal or return cost (rigging, drayage, freight, or a lease-end reconditioning charge), plus any downtime cost while the swap happens. Leaving out removal and downtime is the most common way this comparison undercounts the cost of walking away, so both have their own fields rather than being folded into the replacement price.

    Is any of this uploaded?

    No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, there are no accounts, no cookies and no analytics vendor, and there is no network request in the page at all. A saved comparison stores only the numbers you typed and stays in this browser; reset deletes it. Lease terms and replacement costs are commercially sensitive, which is exactly why none of it leaves the page.

    Does this tool tell me what to do?

    It reports which path this estimate says is cheaper per month of use, and by how much. It cannot weigh cashflow timing, whether a replacement is actually available on short notice, or how much a familiar machine and crew are worth compared to a new one — those are yours to weigh, and the verdict is a starting point for that conversation, not the end of it.

should-i-buy-out-my-equipment-lease.html.text:
← Equipment lease buyout calculator

Should I buy out my equipment lease?

A lease-end payoff letter quotes one number: what the lessor wants to hand you the title. It does not say whether that number is good. The same $14,500 buyout is expensive on a machine worth $9,000 with a year left in it, and cheap on one that would cost $32,000 and four days of downtime to replace. The price is only half a comparison, and the letter never contains the other half.

Open the free buyout calculator

Compare cost per month of use, not prices

The two options buy different things for different lengths of time, so their headline prices are not comparable. Putting them on a common footing takes four numbers:

  • The buyout price, from the payoff letter.
  • The months of use you expect to get if you pay it and keep running the equipment.
  • The all-in cost of replacing it — purchase or new lease, plus removal, plus downtime.
  • The months of use the replacement would give you, which is usually longer, and that difference matters.

Divide each price by its own months and you get two figures that mean the same thing: dollars per month of use. That is the comparison the payoff letter is missing.

Worked example: a 32% premium that is still the better deal

A bakery's five-year lease on a rack oven is ending. The lessor quotes $14,500. A comparable used oven of the same age lists around $11,000, so the buyout is $3,500 over fair market value — a 32% premium, and it reads like an overcharge. The owner expects another 60 months out of the oven. A new equivalent runs $32,000 and would last 120 months; pulling the old one and setting the new one costs $1,800 in rigging and freight, and the swap means 4 days closed at $950 a day.

FigureValue
Buyout price$14,500.00
Remaining useful life if kept60 months
Cost per month — buy out$241.67
Replacement price$32,000.00
Removal and freight$1,800.00
Downtime (4 days × $950)$3,800.00
Total cost to replace$37,600.00
Replacement useful life120 months
Cost per month — replace$313.33
Break-even buyout price$18,800.00
Premium over fair market value$3,500.00 (32%)
Saving from buying out$4,300.00 over 60 months ($71.67/mo)

The premium is real and the buyout is still cheaper. Both things are true at once. Fair market value measures what the oven is worth to sell; it says nothing about what not having an oven would cost. The buyout would have to reach $18,800 — $4,300 above the quote, and 71% above fair market value — before returning it became the better move.

That gap is also the negotiating room. If the lessor will not move off $14,500, the answer is still yes. Knowing break-even sits at $18,800 tells you how hard it is worth pushing, which a payoff letter and a resale listing cannot tell you on their own.

The two costs people leave out

Removal and end-of-term charges. Rigging, drayage, and freight are obvious once you have paid them and invisible before. Less obvious is the return-condition clause: many leases let the lessor bill inspection or reconditioning at the end of term, so returning equipment is rarely free even when the lease is fully paid. Read that clause before you assume the return side starts at zero.

Downtime. The days between the old unit going out and the new one running are a real cost, and one the replacement quote never mentions. In the example above, four days at $950 adds $3,800 — more than the freight. If the replacement could ship late or need commissioning time, treat that figure as a floor.

What the arithmetic cannot weigh

Cost per month is a starting point for the decision, not the decision. Cashflow timing does not appear in it: a business that cannot free up $14,500 this quarter may rationally take the more expensive path. Neither does availability — a replacement that is cheaper on paper and twelve weeks out may not be an option at all. Nor does the value of a machine your crew already knows, with a maintenance history you can read. Run the numbers first, then weigh those against them.

Common questions

Should I buy out my equipment lease or return it?

Compare the two paths on cost per month of use, not on their headline prices. Divide the buyout price by the months of use you expect to get from the equipment, then divide the all-in replacement cost by the months of use you would get from the replacement. Whichever is lower per month is the cheaper path. A payoff letter gives you one of those four numbers, which is why the price on it cannot answer the question on its own.

Can a buyout above fair market value still be worth paying?

Yes, and this is the case people most often get wrong. Fair market value tells you what the equipment is worth to sell; it does not tell you what replacing it would cost you. In the worked example on this page the buyout is 3,500 dollars above fair market value, a 32% premium that looks like an overcharge, and buying out is still cheaper by about 4,300 dollars over the equipment's remaining life, because a replacement plus removal plus downtime comes to 37,600 dollars. Being overcharged relative to resale value and being overcharged relative to your alternative are two different things.

What is the break-even buyout price?

It is the buyout price at which paying and walking away cost exactly the same per month of use. Below it, buying out is cheaper; above it, replacing is. It is the number worth negotiating against, because it is derived from your alternative rather than from the lessor's schedule. In the worked example the quoted buyout is 14,500 dollars and break-even is 18,800 dollars, so there is 4,300 dollars of room before walking away becomes the better move.

What costs belong on the return-and-replace side?

The replacement's purchase price or total new lease cost, plus removal and return costs, plus downtime. Removal covers rigging, drayage, freight, and any end-of-term inspection or reconditioning charge your lease allows the lessor to bill. Downtime is the days of lost production between the old unit leaving and the new one running, priced at what a day is worth to you. Leaving these two out is the most common way this comparison undercounts the cost of walking away, and in the worked example they add 5,600 dollars to a 32,000 dollar replacement.

Where do I get the fair market value and useful life numbers?

Both are your own estimates rather than a lookup. For fair market value, a comparable dealer listing, auction result, or classified ad for the same make, model, and age is usually close enough, and a written appraisal is worth it when the number is large. For remaining useful life, your maintenance history and how hard the unit has been run matter more than its age on paper. Both drive the verdict directly, so a rough guess in either one should be treated as producing a rough verdict, not a precise one.

Does a lease that settles at fair market value have to match an appraisal?

That depends on what your lease actually says, and the distinction is worth reading before you pay. Some leases set the end-of-term option at true fair market value; others set it on a fixed schedule agreed at signing, which can drift well above what the equipment is worth by the time you exercise it, especially on fast-depreciating gear. If your contract specifies fair market value and the lessor's figure sits well above comparable listings, that is a question to raise before paying rather than after.

Run it on your own payoff letter

The calculator takes the same inputs used above and reports cost per month on both paths, the break-even buyout price, and the premium over fair market value. It runs entirely in your browser.

Open the free buyout calculator

vs-comparing-the-buyout-price-to-fair-ma.text:
← Equipment lease buyout calculator

This calculator vs. comparing the buyout price to fair market value

A price below fair market value is not the same question as a price worth paying.

The habit most payoff letters get checked against is fair market value: is the quoted buyout close to, above, or below what the equipment is worth right now? It is the fastest sanity check available — get an appraisal or a comparable listing, compare it to the number on the letter, and decide from the gap.

That check answers one question — is this price close to the equipment's value — and says nothing about how many more months of service that price buys, what a replacement would cost, or how long the replacement would last. This calculator starts from the same payoff letter but converts both paths to cost per month of use: the buyout price against the useful life you have left, and a replacement's cost against its own expected life, plus optional removal and downtime costs. A buyout can price well under fair market value and still be the more expensive path per month, and a buyout priced above fair market value can still be the cheaper one.

What each check answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Is this buyout price reasonable next to what the equipment is worth right now? Comparing it to a fair-market-value estimate — a useful sanity check on the price alone.
Is paying the buyout actually the cheaper path once remaining life and a real replacement enter the picture? This calculator — it converts both paths to cost per month of use and reports the cheaper one.
What buyout price would make the two paths cost the same per month? This calculator's break-even buyout price — the number worth negotiating against, not the fair-market-value estimate.
What does removal, downtime, or a replacement's all-in cost do to the decision? This calculator — both have their own fields rather than being folded into a headline price.

A bargain that is not one

Using this calculator's own figures: an $8,000 buyout quoted against equipment appraised at $10,000 fair market value — 20% below FMV, a number most people would read as settled — on equipment with 6 months of useful life left, compared against a $15,000 replacement good for 60 months. The buyout costs $1,333.33 per month to keep; the replacement costs $250.00 per month. Despite pricing well under fair market value, the buyout is the more expensive path by 5.33 times per month, and keeping the leased equipment costs $6,500 more over its remaining life than returning it and replacing it. The break-even buyout price here is $1,500 — over five times below the $8,000 actually quoted.

Common questions

Why can a buyout below fair market value still be the wrong deal?

Because fair market value prices the equipment, not the months of use you are actually buying. A buyout below FMV looks like a bargain on the payoff letter, but if the equipment only has a few months of useful life left and a replacement would run for years at a similar or lower price, the buyout can cost far more per month of use than walking away and replacing it. Using this calculator's own figures: a $8,000 buyout on equipment appraised at $10,000 fair market value -- 20% below FMV -- with 6 months of useful life left, against a $15,000 replacement good for 60 months, costs $1,333.33 per month to keep versus $250.00 per month to replace. The buyout is the worse deal by 5.33 times per month despite pricing 20% under fair market value.

What does comparing the buyout price to fair market value alone leave out?

Remaining useful life, replacement cost, and how long the replacement would last. Fair market value answers one question -- is this price close to what the equipment is worth right now -- and says nothing about how many more months of service that price buys, what a replacement costs, or how long the replacement lasts. Two buyouts priced identically against fair market value can be opposite decisions once useful life and a replacement's cost and lifespan enter the comparison.

How big is the gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own figures: an $8,000 buyout against a $10,000 fair-market-value estimate reads as a 20% discount, which most people would take as settled. But at 6 months of remaining useful life, that buyout costs $1,333.33 per month to keep. A $15,000 replacement lasting 60 months costs $250.00 per month. Keeping the leased equipment costs $6,500 more over its remaining life than returning it and replacing it -- the break-even buyout price for this comparison is $1,500, over five times below the $8,000 actually quoted.

Is comparing the buyout price to fair market value ever the right check?

It is a reasonable sanity check on the price itself -- a buyout well above fair market value is worth a second look at the lease contract before paying it. What it cannot tell you is whether paying that price is the cheaper path once remaining useful life and a real replacement's cost and lifespan are on the table, and by then a payoff letter is often already close to due.

Does this calculator know my equipment's fair market value or what a replacement costs?

No. It has no appraisal data, no equipment pricing feed, and no knowledge of your lease terms. It takes the buyout price, your own estimate of fair market value, remaining useful life, a replacement's cost and expected life, and optional removal and downtime costs, and converts both paths to cost per month of use -- the arithmetic a fair-market-value comparison skips, not an appraisal.

vs-crest-capital.html.text:
← Equipment Lease Buyout Calculator

This calculator vs. Crest Capital's lease calculator

One prices a new lease before it starts. The other compares buying out a lease that is already ending against returning the equipment and replacing it, in cost per month of use.

What Crest Capital's calculator is

Crest Capital is a national equipment financing and leasing lender, founded in 1989 and headquartered in Alpharetta, Georgia, that finances equipment, vehicles, and software for small and mid-size businesses. Its site offers a free calculator that takes the cost of one piece of new equipment and estimates the monthly payment for financing or leasing it through Crest Capital — a tool for the start of a lease, typically as a first step toward submitting an application.

What this calculator is

This page is for the other end of a lease: the payoff letter that arrives when an existing lease is ending, quoting a buyout price. It does not estimate a lease payment and is not tied to any lender. Enter the quoted buyout price, the equipment's estimated fair market value, how many months of use it has left, and the all-in cost of a replacement — purchase or new lease, plus removal and expected downtime — and it reports the cost per month of use on each path, the break-even buyout price, and how the quoted buyout compares to fair market value. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, and there is no application to submit.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I'm about to lease or finance a new piece of equipment and need a monthly payment estimate before applying. Crest Capital's calculator or a comparable lender's — pricing a new lease is exactly its job, and this calculator has no financing terms of its own to offer.
My existing lease is ending and I have a payoff letter quoting a buyout price. Is it a good deal? This calculator — a buyout price alone means nothing without something to compare it to. Enter the equipment's fair market value, remaining useful life, and replacement cost, and it converts both paths to cost per month of use.
I want to know the exact buyout price at which paying it and replacing the equipment cost the same. This calculator — it reports the break-even buyout price, the number worth negotiating against, not the figure printed on the payoff letter. Crest Capital's calculator has no concept of a buyout at all.
I don't want to enter lease and replacement figures into a lender's site before I know whether the buyout is worth paying. This calculator — it needs only the numbers already on the payoff letter and a replacement quote, and sends nothing to Crest Capital or anyone else.

Neither tool replaces the other. A business leasing a new asset for the first time still needs a lender's own payment estimate — that is what Crest Capital's calculator, or a comparable lender's, is for. Once that same lease is ending and a payoff letter is in hand, this page is where you check whether the buyout is actually cheaper than walking away, before paying it.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Crest Capital's lease calculator?

They answer different questions, at different ends of a lease. Crest Capital, a national equipment financing and leasing lender founded in 1989 and headquartered in Alpharetta, Georgia, offers a calculator on its own site that estimates the monthly payment for financing or leasing one piece of new equipment, vehicle, or software — a first step toward starting a lease, typically through Crest Capital. This calculator is for the other end of a lease: the payoff letter that arrives when an existing lease is ending, offering a buyout price. It does not estimate a payment at all — it converts the quoted buyout and a return-and-replace alternative to cost per month of use, using the equipment's remaining useful life and a replacement's all-in cost, so the two paths are comparable on a common footing instead of a bare price on a letter. If you are starting a new lease, Crest Capital's calculator or a comparable lender's is built for that. If you are holding a buyout offer on an existing lease and deciding whether to pay it or walk away, this page answers that instead.

Is this page affiliated with Crest Capital?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Crest Capital. Crest Capital is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

This page is a factual comparison of what each tool does, not an evaluation of which is better. Details about Crest Capital above describe the general shape of its business and calculator as publicly described at the time of writing and may have changed — verify against Crest Capital's own site before deciding, and no specific rate, fee, or price for Crest Capital's financing is stated here.

vs-lendzero.html.text:
← Equipment lease buyout calculator

This calculator vs. Lendzero

Different moments in the same lease: one sizes it before you sign, the other checks the payoff letter after.

Lendzero publishes a one-dollar-buyout equipment lease calculator, described on its own site as covering the three common lease structures — one-dollar buyout, fair market value (FMV), and 10% buyout — for a lease you have not yet signed: enter the equipment cost, term, and rate, and it estimates the payment and buyout you would be agreeing to.

That is a useful tool at signing time, and a different job from the one this page does. This calculator has no payment schedule, no rate factor, and nothing to size a new lease. It starts later, at the moment a lease is already ending: you are holding a payoff letter with one buyout number on it, and the question is no longer "what will the payment be" but "is this buyout worth paying, or is returning the equipment and replacing it actually cheaper?" It converts both paths to cost per month of use on a common footing and reports the break-even buyout price — the number worth negotiating against, not the figure on the letter.

What each tool answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I'm about to sign a new equipment lease — what will the payment and buyout look like under a one-dollar, FMV, or 10% buyout? Lendzero's calculator — sizing a lease before signing is exactly what it is built for.
My lease is ending and the payoff letter quotes a buyout price — is paying it cheaper than returning the equipment and replacing it? This calculator — it compares both paths on cost per month of use and names the break-even buyout price.
How does the quoted buyout compare to what the equipment is actually worth? This calculator — it signs the gap against a fair-market-value estimate you supply, so a buyout priced above FMV is easy to spot.
What does removal, downtime, or a replacement's all-in cost do to the decision? This calculator — both have their own fields rather than being folded into a headline price.

Nothing here is a claim about Lendzero's pricing, terms, or accuracy for the job it does — sizing a lease before signing is not the question this page answers, so there is nothing to compare it on. This calculator is free and needs no account.
